summary: The Marshall Islands is an island nation in the central Pacific made up of 29 atolls; after World War II the United States conducted nuclear tests at Bikini and Enewetak atolls.

ranking.name: United Church of Christ
ranking.description: The United Church of Christ traces to the church established in 1857 by American Congregationalist missionaries from Hawaii; after the local chiefs converted, Protestantism spread rapidly in the Marshall Islands. It is the oldest and most influential church in the Marshall Islands, and church activities are closely bound up with community life and festivals.

ranking.name: Assemblies of God
ranking.description: The Assemblies of God is a Pentecostal church introduced from the United States in the 20th century, emphasizing the experience of the Holy Spirit and fervent worship. As American influence deepened after World War II, the Assemblies of God attracted many believers in urban areas such as Majuro and became the second-largest denomination.

ranking.name: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints
ranking.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (Mormons) was introduced to the Marshall Islands in the late 20th century and attracted followers through missionaries and education programs. Because under the Compact of Free Association Marshall Islanders can freely migrate to the United States, many believers have established ties with Mormon communities in the United States.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Catholicism was introduced by German missionaries during the German colonial period (1885–1914), after which American Jesuits took over. The Catholic Church runs primary and secondary schools in places such as Majuro and has made an important contribution to education, but the number of believers is relatively small.

religion.background: The indigenous people of the Marshall Islands traditionally worshipped ancestral spirits and nature spirits, and the chiefs (iroij) held both religious and political authority. In 1857 American Congregationalist missionaries came from Hawaii to Ebon Atoll and began spreading Protestantism, and the conversion of the local chiefs made Christianity spread rapidly. Germany colonized from 1885, Japan ruled from 1914, and after World War II the islands became part of the U.S.-administered Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands. From 1946 to 1958 the United States conducted nuclear tests at Bikini and Enewetak atolls, which had a profound effect on local society. After independence in 1986, Christianity is at the center of social life, and churches play an important role in the community.

language.official: Marshallese and English are the official languages.

ranking.name: Marshallese
ranking.description: Marshallese is the language of the indigenous people of the Marshall Islands; after missionaries devised a writing system for it in the 19th century, churches and schools promoted literacy. Since the citizens are almost all Marshallese, Marshallese is widely used in homes, churches, communities and parliament, and is the mother tongue of the great majority.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: English dates from the U.S. trusteeship period after World War II (1947–1986) and is one of the official languages, used in government, law and higher education. Under the Compact of Free Association, Marshallese can freely migrate to the United States, and many families have relatives in places such as Arkansas and Hawaii, so English ability is increasingly important.

language.history: Marshallese belongs to the Micronesian group of the Oceanic branch of the Austronesian language family and is divided into two major dialects, Ratak (sunrise) and Ralik (sunset), corresponding to the two chains of atolls in the east and west of the Marshall Islands. In the mid-19th century American missionaries devised a writing system for Marshallese in the Latin alphabet and translated the Bible. German and Japanese were introduced during the German colonial period (1885–1914) and the Japanese period (1914–1944) respectively, leaving a small number of loanwords; after World War II, under American trusteeship, English became the language of education and government. After independence in 1986 Marshallese and English became joint official languages.

ranking.name: Breadfruit
ranking.description: Breadfruit can be roasted, boiled, fried, or fermented into a paste for preservation, and is one of the traditional staples. It has a potato-like texture and is rich in starch, an important traditional staple.
ranking.history: Breadfruit spread across the Pacific thousands of years ago with the voyaging migrations of the Austronesian peoples, and in the Marshall Islands it is one of the traditional staples. In the past people fermented breadfruit and buried it in the ground for storage as reserve food during typhoons or droughts, and it was also provisions for long voyages. After World War II, American aid brought large imports of rice and canned food, the share of traditional foods fell, and health problems such as diabetes increased, and in recent years the government has promoted a return to the traditional diet.

ranking.name: Pandanus
ranking.description: The fruit of the pandanus (screwpine) can be chewed directly, or cooked into a paste or dried into long-keeping dried fruit. The flesh is sweet and fibrous and is a precious source of food on the atolls.
ranking.history: The pandanus tree is salt- and drought-tolerant and one of the few plants able to grow on the barren sandy soil of atolls, and Marshallese have bred many varieties. Pandanus fruit can be processed into dried fruit (jāānkun) that keeps for a long time and was provisions during traditional voyages. Pandanus leaves can also be woven into mats, sails and roofs, and the Marshallese traditional navigation technology relied on sails woven from pandanus leaves.

ranking.name: Coconut
ranking.description: Coconut flesh, water, milk and oil are ubiquitous in Marshallese cooking, and coconut tree sap can also be made into syrup. It is an important source of food and drink for atoll dwellers.
ranking.history: The coconut palm is called the "tree of life"; on the atolls of the Marshall Islands, coconut is a source of water, food, oil and building material. During the German colonial period (1885–1914) coconuts began to be planted on a large scale and copra was exported, and copra is still an important source of income for outer-island residents today. The coconut holds an important place in Marshallese traditional knowledge, songs and rituals.

ranking.name: Taro
ranking.description: Giant swamp taro is cultivated in dug pits, and after harvest is roasted, boiled or mashed. It has a soft texture with a light sweetness and is an honored food at festivals.
ranking.history: Growing taro on an atoll requires digging pits to reach the underground freshwater lens and improving the soil with leaf compost, which shows the wisdom of Pacific islanders in adapting to the atoll environment. Taro is an honored food at important ceremonies such as weddings, funerals and a first child's first birthday (kemem). In recent years, rising sea levels and saltwater intrusion into the pits have seriously threatened traditional taro growing.

ranking.name: Coconut crab
ranking.description: A giant land hermit crab, whose body can grow very large, with sweet meat, usually boiled or grilled. The crab meat and the fat of the abdomen have a coconut aroma and are regarded as a delicacy.
ranking.history: The coconut crab can crack open coconuts with its powerful claws, hence its name. In the Marshall Islands, catching coconut crabs is a traditional skill, often done at night, and the crab is regarded as a delicacy for festivals or entertaining guests. Because of population growth and overharvesting, coconut crabs have become increasingly scarce on inhabited atolls, and in addition coconut crabs from the nuclear test areas have at times been unfit to eat because of radioactive contamination.
